newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Sharp drop in oil costs behind lower S.African PPI.
newsitem.headline: Sharp drop in oil costs behind lower S.African PPI.

text.p: A sharp drop in cost of imported crude oil was the main factor behind an unexpectedly large drop in South African producer price inflation in April, th Central Statistical Service said (CSS).

The PPI for imported commodities showed an annual rate of increase of just 5.4 percent in April, 4.7 percentage points lower than the corresponding annual rate in March and the lowest annual rate recorded in seven months.
The main contributor to this decline was a 20.2 percent monthly fall in the imported price of crude petroleum.

Wide variations in the oil component of PPI have been questioned by economists in the past. But the CSS said in a statement on Tuesday that Customs and Excise, which supplies the basic date, had confirmed this large price decrease.
"Among a large number of recorded consignments, of different sizes, an appreciable price decrease was reflected for every one," the CSS said.
April's all-commodities producer price index rose 0.4 percent month-on-month and 8.8 percent year-on-year, far better than the consensus of 0.9 and 9.5 forecast by economists.

Economists welcomed the figure which they said confirmed the belief that South African inflation had now peaked, with the beneficial effects of the rand's strength this year clearly feeding through to slower price increases.
Standard Bank's economics unit said PPI should now fall below seven percent before the end of the year.
Herman van Papendrop, economist at SMK Securities, also saw PPI at seven percent by the year-end.

He said the data was encouraging for interest rate cut hopes, although the authorities would remain cautious until they had assessed the impact of the next step in relaxing exchange controls which takes effect from July 1.
"It's good news for interest rates but July 1 is still the big question-mark," van Papendorp said.

Residents will be allowed to invest an as-yet unstated amount offshore from next month. If the move goes smoothly, analysts believe it could encourage the Reserve Bank to ease monetary policy, especially after evidence of a sharp slowdown in the economy in the first quarter.
On the bond market, yields pushed lower as traders took heart from the better-than expected figure, helping the market recover most of its early losses.
By 0940 GMT the key R150 gilt was yielding 14.605 percent from a morning worst level of 14.665 before the data and Monday's late level of 14.590
"A few people got short this morning after the rand trouble on Monday and now I think they'll scramble on this figure," said one bond dealer.

The monthly producer inflation rate for imported commodities fell 3.2 percent, thanks to the drop in crude oil. But this was offset by the 1.2 percent increase in the more important locally-produced component, resulting in the all-commodity month-on-month increase of 0.4 percent.

Relatively large monthly increases were seen for various items including agricultural food products (+1.0 percent), fishing products (+4.1), food at manufacturing (+0.9), beverages (+7.0) and tobacco products (+17.0).
